items.title: Compute float64 exp, sin, cos and erf in double
items.body:
## Proposed changes

Fixes #4158.

`exp`, `sin`, `cos` and `erf` in `mlx/backend/cpu/simd/math.h` are hand-rolled
float32 approximations, and they convert their input to `Simd<float, N>`
unconditionally. float64 therefore gets float32 accuracy:

| max rel. error, float64 | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `exp` | 3.00e-07 | 0.00e+00 |
| `sin` | 7.75e-07 | 0.00e+00 |
| `cos` | 3.42e-04 | 0.00e+00 |
| `erf` | 9.44e-04 | 0.00e+00 |

`exp` is worse than imprecise, because it also inherited float's saturation
points, so a float64 array returns the wrong value outright:

```
exp(100.0)  -> inf   (should be 2.688e+43)
exp(709.0)  -> inf   (should be 8.218e+307)
exp(-200.0) -> 0     (should be 1.384e-87)
```

This routes double through libm and leaves float32 untouched.

Worth flagging: the existing `test_unary_ops` in `python/tests/test_double.py`
asserts `allclose(y, y_double.astype(mx.float32, mx.cpu))` — it compares the
float64 result against the float32 one, so it could not catch any of this.

### Performance

This is a real cost. 2^20 elements, M2 Pro, best of 7 runs:

| | float32 (unchanged) | float64 before | float64 after |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `exp` | 0.437 -> 0.438 ms | 0.573 ms | 5.908 ms |
| `sin` | 0.804 -> 0.807 ms | 1.067 ms | 6.659 ms |
| `cos` | 0.786 -> 0.791 ms | 1.032 ms | 6.743 ms |
| `erf` | 0.877 -> 0.878 ms | 1.160 ms | 11.641 ms |

float32 is unchanged, as expected from a compile-time branch. The old float64
speed was the speed of computing the wrong answer.

I checked whether that speed can be recovered. Accelerate's vectorized double
math (`simd::exp` / `simd::erf` on `double4`) measured no faster than scalar
libm on this machine — 2.456 vs 2.558 ms for `exp`, 9.653 vs 9.951 ms for `erf`,
with bit-identical results — so the cost looks intrinsic to evaluating these at
double precision rather than a poor choice of implementation. Happy to take
direction if you would prefer a different trade-off here.

`erfinv` still narrows to float. It has no libm equivalent and would need a
double precision polynomial, so I left it for a separate change rather than
half-do it.

### Testing

Two new tests in `python/tests/test_double.py`: one pins the four ops to double
accuracy against numpy, one pins the range of `exp`. Both fail before this
change and pass after.

- Full Python suite: 821 tests, no new failures.
- Full C++ suite: 247 cases, 3326 assertions, all pass.

Built CPU-only (`MLX_BUILD_METAL=OFF`). float64 is CPU-only in MLX, so that is
where this behaviour lives, but note the GPU suite was not run on my machine.

## Checklist

- [x] I have read the [CONTRIBUTING](https://github.com/ml-explore/mlx/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md) document
- [x] I have run `pre-commit run --all-files` to format my code / installed pre-commit prior to committing changes
- [x] I have added tests that prove my fix is effective or that my feature works
- [ ] I have updated the necessary documentation (if needed) — no documentation change needed, there is no API change

items.title: [BUG] `mx.sin` / `mx.cos` / `mx.exp` on float64 return float32-class accuracy (max rel err 3.2e-04 for cos)
items.body:
**Describe the bug**
For a `float64` input, `mx.sin`, `mx.cos` and `mx.exp` return results whose **relative** error is of order
`1e-7`  (i.e. float32-class) while the returned dtype is `float64`. `mx.tan`, `mx.log` and `mx.sqrt` on
the same inputs are correctly rounded (~1e-16), so this is specific to these three functions rather than a
general float64 limitation.

`mx.cos` is the worst at **3.2e-04** max relative error, which is ~1e12x float64 epsilon.

**To Reproduce**

```python
import mlx.core as mx, numpy as np, mpmath as mp
mp.mp.dps = 60
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
xs = rng.uniform(-3, 3, 2000)

with mx.stream(mx.cpu):
    A = mx.array(xs, dtype=mx.float64)
    for name, fn, ref in (("sin", mx.sin, mp.sin), ("cos", mx.cos, mp.cos), ("exp", mx.exp, mp.exp),
                          ("tan", mx.tan, mp.tan), ("log", mx.log, mp.log), ("sqrt", mx.sqrt, mp.sqrt)):
        src = np.abs(xs) if name in ("log", "sqrt") else xs
        B = np.asarray(fn(mx.abs(A) if name in ("log", "sqrt") else A))
        rel = max(abs(float((mp.mpf(float(B[i])) - ref(mp.mpf(float(src[i])))) / ref(mp.mpf(float(src[i])))))
                  for i in range(len(xs)))
        print(f"mx.{name:5s} float64 max relative error = {rel:.3e}")
```

```
mx.sin   float64 max relative error = 7.746e-07     <-- float32-class
mx.cos   float64 max relative error = 3.206e-04     <-- float32-class, and 1e12x float64 eps
mx.exp   float64 max relative error = 2.932e-07     <-- float32-class
mx.tan   float64 max relative error = 3.077e-16     ok
mx.log   float64 max relative error = 2.452e-16     ok
mx.sqrt  float64 max relative error = 1.094e-16     ok
```

Single-value form, if that is easier to triage:

```python
import mlx.core as mx, numpy as np, mpmath as mp
with mx.stream(mx.cpu):
    a = mx.array([1.0], dtype=mx.float64)
    print(float(np.asarray(mx.cos(a))[0]))   # actual:  0.5403022766113281   <- float32 value
print(float(mp.cos(mp.mpf(1))))              # correct: 0.5403023058681398
```

**Expected behavior**
A `float64` input should give a `float64`-accurate result, within a few ULP (~1e-16 relative), as `tan`,
`log` and `sqrt` already do.

**Environment**
`mlx 0.32.0` · python 3.12 · Apple M2 (arm64), macOS · float64 evaluated under `with mx.stream(mx.cpu)`
(float64 is CPU-only) · reference: `mpmath` at 60 decimal digits.

items.title: Use precise::exp in Sigmoid so compiled and eager sigmoid agree
items.body:
`mx.sigmoid` returns a different, less accurate result inside an `mx.compile`d
graph than it does eagerly on Metal.

```python
import mlx.core as mx
x = mx.linspace(-12, 12, 4001)
eager = mx.sigmoid(x)
fused = mx.compile(lambda a: mx.sigmoid(a) * 1.0)(x)
mx.eval(eager, fused)
print(mx.array_equal(fused, eager))   # False
```

On this sweep 1362 of 4001 float32 elements differ, and the compiled result has
5.13x the maximum relative error against a float64 reference (8.0910e-07 vs
1.5768e-07). In bfloat16 the two also disagree; I did not characterise the
bfloat16 error ratio.

## Cause

`Sigmoid` spells an unqualified `metal::exp`:

```cpp
// mlx/backend/metal/kernels/unary_ops.h
struct Sigmoid {
  template <typename T>
  T operator()(T x) thread {
    auto y = 1 / (1 + metal::exp(metal::abs(x)));
    return (x < 0) ? y : 1 - y;
  }
};
```

`Exp` in the same header already uses `metal::precise::exp`.

The prebuilt `mlx.metallib` is compiled with `-fno-fast-math`, and there the
unqualified spelling gives the precise result — which is why eager `mx.sigmoid`
is accurate. `Compiled` primitives are instead built at runtime, and there the
same text gives the fast approximation. Note that `CompileOptions::math_mode`
already defaults to `MathMode::Safe` and `set_compile_options` sets only
`mathMode`; math mode is not the control that selects between the fast and
precise floating-point function sets, so defaulting it to safe does not prevent
this.

Evidence that the `exp` spelling is what moves, rather than fusion
(reassociation, contraction, intermediate precision): a hand-written
`mx.fast.metal_kernel` carrying the struct body verbatim reproduces the
*compiled* result bit for bit; substituting `metal::precise::exp` reproduces the
*eager* result bit for bit; and `metal::fast::exp` is bit-identical to the
unqualified spelling. That trio isolates the spelling inside one JIT
environment, with no fusion partner involved.

This is not a proof that fusion contributes nothing — but multiplying by exactly
`1.0` offers no reassociation or FMA opportunity, and could not explain exact
bit-for-bit agreement with an independently hand-written fast-`exp` kernel.

## Scope

`Sigmoid` is not the only unqualified transcendental in these headers —
`LogAddExp` and the complex `Power` path in `binary_ops.h`, `cexpf.h`, the
`log1p` helpers in `utils.h`, and `erfinv` in `erf.h` are in the same position.
This PR changes only `Sigmoid`, the one with a demonstrated user-visible
divergence. The others are left alone deliberately; happy to widen it if you
would rather fix the class.

## Effect on nn.silu

`nn.silu` is `@partial(mx.compile)`, so today it gets the fast sigmoid. This
patch changes its output. It changes it to agree with the eager path:

| | nn.silu vs fp64 | eager `x * mx.sigmoid(x)` vs fp64 | elements differing |
|---|---|---|---|
| before | 8.2263e-07 | 1.9370e-07 | 1332 / 4001 |
| after | 1.9370e-07 | 1.9370e-07 | 0 / 4001 |

Measured on one M5 Max, float32, over that sweep. Anyone pinning exact `nn.silu`
outputs in that configuration will see them move. I have not characterised the
change on other devices or dtypes, and have not added an `nn.silu` regression
test — say the word if you want one.

## float16 is unaffected

Exhaustively, over all 65536 half bit patterns including NaN, Inf, subnormals
and -0: `fast::exp` and `precise::exp` inside this expression produce
bit-identical float16 results (0 differ, including all 2046 NaN inputs). The
substitution is inert for float16.

## Performance

`precise::exp` is the more expensive implementation.

Isolated, in an `exp`-dominated loop (512 `exp` per thread over 2^20 threads,
hand-written kernels, best of 60, M5 Max, float32):

| | min | median |
|---|---:|---:|
| `metal::fast::exp` | 0.549 ms | 0.756 ms |
| `metal::precise::exp` | 0.727 ms | 0.823 ms |
| `metal::exp` (unqualified) | 0.541 ms | 0.592 ms |

1.33x on the minima. The unqualified row landing near `fast::exp` is consistent
with the bit-identity result above, though the medians are noisy enough that I
would not lean on the timing as independent evidence.

**I have no valid end-to-end before/after number.** Two attempts failed and I am
reporting them rather than the third: in the first, a control computation proven
bit-identical across both builds itself moved 0.1979 -> 0.2621 ms, so the
comparison was noise; in the second, a chain of 32 and then 384 sigmoids timed
identically to a sigmoid-free chain of the same length (0.3800 / 0.3800 ms at
384), so the benchmark had no sensitivity to `exp` cost at all. I could not
construct an elementwise graph in which the difference was measurable. I am not
claiming the end-to-end cost is zero.

## Testing

One machine (M5 Max, macOS 26.6.2, Xcode 26.6), one checkout of main at
b6368984b, one venv. Both arms are that same tree rebuilt in place — stock,
then patched, then reverted and rebuilt to re-confirm the baseline.

- Added a regression test asserting compiled sigmoid equals eager sigmoid in
  float32 and bfloat16. It fails before the patch and passes after.
- After the patch, eager and fused-compiled sigmoid are bit-identical, and the
  eager result is unchanged from before the patch.
- `test_compile.py`, `test_ops.py`, `test_fast.py`, `test_bf16.py` pass on both
  arms. `test_nn.py` has one failure, `test_sin_pe`
  (`0.000858784 not less than 1e-05`), which reproduced 3/3 on the unpatched
  build as well, so it is not introduced by this patch. It is a sin/cos test and
  the magnitude resembles #4411.

Not verified on M1-M4 or on iOS/visionOS.

---

This issue was discovered by me during fused-kernel development QA, augmented with CC and OAI.

When mapping back test data to stock, we discovered misalignment and discovered the source of divergence was present upstream; we applied local fixes but this issue appears to impact correctness upstream. I don't know if this is an explicit tradeoff that was accepted for performance, suspect that it's not.

items.title: [BUG] `x ** 2` is less accurate than `x * x` (0.938 vs 0.500 ULP) and is lane-dependent
items.body:
**Describe the bug**
`x ** 2` (and `mx.power(x, 2)`) route through a general power kernel instead of a multiply. In float32 it is worse than `x * x` on 9742/20000 random draws and better on zero. On float64 it is lane-dependent. `mx.square(x)` is already bit-identical to `x * x` in both precisions, and behaves correctly. `**` just is not reaching it.

**To Reproduce**

```python
import mlx.core as mx, numpy as np, mpmath as mp
mp.mp.dps = 60
rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
xs = rng.uniform(-3, 3, 20000)

with mx.stream(mx.cpu):
    A = mx.array(xs, dtype=mx.float64)
    sq, mul, pw = mx.square(A), A * A, A ** 2
    mx.eval(sq, mul, pw)
print("float64: mx.square == x*x :", np.array_equal(np.asarray(sq), np.asarray(mul)))
print("float64: x**2      == x*x :", np.array_equal(np.asarray(pw), np.asarray(mul)),
      f"({int((np.asarray(pw) != np.asarray(mul)).sum())}/20000 differ)")

x32 = mx.array(xs.astype(np.float32))
print("float32: x**2 == x*x :", np.array_equal(np.asarray(x32 ** 2), np.asarray(x32 * x32)),
      f"({int((np.asarray(x32**2) != np.asarray(x32*x32)).sum())}/20000 differ)")

def ulps(g):
    return max(abs(float((mp.mpf(float(g[i])) - mp.mpf(float(xs[i]))**2)
                         / mp.mpf(np.spacing(abs(np.float64(g[i])))))) for i in range(2000))
print(f"float64 max |ULP| : x*x {ulps(np.asarray(mul)):.3f}   mx.square {ulps(np.asarray(sq)):.3f}   "
      f"x**2 {ulps(np.asarray(pw)):.3f}")
```


```
float64: mx.square == x*x : True
float64: x**2      == x*x : False   (2620/20000 differ)
float32: x**2      == x*x : False   (9742/20000 differ)
float64 max |ULP| : x*x 0.500   mx.square 0.500   x**2 0.938
```

**Expected behavior**
`x ** 2` should be as accurate as `x * x`, i.e. lowered to a multiply. Likewise `x ** 3` → `x*x*x`,
`x ** 0.5` → `sqrt`, `x ** -1` → reciprocal (lane-dependent submitted as a separate issue).
(`x**0.5` on 110/400, `x**-1` on 51/400).


For **exponent 3 and 1.5** the naive algebraic expansion is slightly *worse* than the current power kernel
at the extremes, over 2000 draws vs mpmath:

| exponent | `mx.power` mean/max ULP | algebraic mean/max ULP |
|---|---|---|
| 1.5 | 0.334 / 0.979 | `x*mx.sqrt(x)` 0.347 / **1.165** |
| 3   | 0.344 / 0.979 | `x*x*x` 0.343 / **1.229** |

items.title: Improve CPU float64 exp SIMD accuracy
items.body:
## Summary

This is narrow partial progress for #3047: it improves CPU `float64` accuracy for `exp` by adding a double-precision SIMD polynomial path in `mlx/backend/cpu/simd/math.h`.

It intentionally does **not** claim to fix the other fp64 unary ops mentioned in #3047 (`sin`, `cos`, `erf`, `erfinv`). I checked the prior closed PR #3058 and kept this patch aligned with the maintainer feedback there: this is not a scalar element-wise `std::exp` fallback.

## Evidence

Pre-change, CPU `float64` `exp([0.1, 0.5, 0.9, 1.25])` showed fp32-scale error from another local checkout at `0.32.0.dev20260621+5abdd04b`:

- max absolute error: `2.783627603974992e-07`

Post-change, after rebuilding the local editable MLX package from this branch:

- `python -m pip install -e . --no-build-isolation` passed
- CPU `float64` exp max absolute error: `4.440892098500626e-16`
- softmax-like fp64 exp-normalization max absolute error: `1.3877787807814457e-17`
- `python -m pytest python/tests/test_double.py -q` passed: `10 passed`
- `python -m pytest python/tests/test_ops.py -q -k 'exp or softmax'` passed: `7 passed, 134 deselected`

I also added a C++ `ops_tests.cpp` regression that checks `float64` `exp` against `std::exp` at `1e-12` tolerance. I could not run the C++ doctest binary locally because the editable build tree did not include the C++ test executable / doctest headers, so this is draft until that is covered by CI or a local C++ test build.

## Notes

- Related issue: #3047
- Prior attempt checked: #3058
- This is a draft until C++ test coverage is confirmed.

items.title: [Metal] fp32 matmul truncates operands to ~11 bits on applegpu_g17s (M5) since 0.31.0 — accurate on g15d/M4, accurate at M=1
items.body:
## Summary

Since **0.31.0**, `mx.matmul` on **float32** truncates its operands to roughly 11 significand
bits on **`applegpu_g17s`** (M5 generation) whenever the operation is a true GEMM — that is,
when both M >= 2 and N >= 2. At M = 1 an accurate GEMV path is dispatched instead, so
single-row inference hides the fault completely.

The same versions are **accurate on other architectures** (`applegpu_g15d` / M3 Ultra, and an
M4), so this appears to be a kernel selected only for the newer architecture rather than a
general regression.

Only float32 is affected. bf16 and fp16 results are bit-identical before and after the change,
which is consistent with 8 and 10 mantissa bits already sitting at or below the truncation
point.

## Repro

```python
import numpy as np, mlx.core as mx

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
W = rng.standard_normal((256, 1024)).astype(np.float32)
for M in (1, 8):
    A = rng.standard_normal((M, 256)).astype(np.float32)
    truth = A.astype(np.float64) @ W.astype(np.float64)          # float64 arbiter
    with mx.stream(mx.gpu):
        got = np.array(mx.matmul(mx.array(A), mx.array(W)), copy=True)
    print(M, mx.device_info()["architecture"],
          f'{np.abs(got - truth).max() / np.abs(truth).max():.3e}')
```

On an M5 Max (`applegpu_g17s`), mlx 0.32.2:

```
1 applegpu_g17s 1.299e-07
8 applegpu_g17s 8.302e-04      <-- expected ~1e-07
```

## Version bracket — same machine, only mlx varied

| mlx | M=8 relative error vs float64 |
|---|---|
| 0.29.3 | 2.183e-07 |
| 0.30.0 | 2.183e-07 |
| 0.30.1 | 2.183e-07 |
| **0.31.0** | **8.302e-04** |
| 0.31.1 | 8.302e-04 |
| 0.31.2 | 8.302e-04 |
| 0.32.0 | 8.302e-04 |
| 0.32.2 | 8.302e-04 |

Introduced in **0.31.0** and present through 0.32.2.

## Architecture gating — same mlx, different hardware

| device | `mx.device_info()["architecture"]` | mlx | M=8 error |
|---|---|---|---|
| M5 Max | `applegpu_g17s` | 0.32.2 | 8.302e-04 |
| M3 Ultra | `applegpu_g15d` | 0.32.1 | 6.151e-07 |
| M4 (Air) | — | 0.31.1 | 6.151e-07 |

`MLX_METAL_GPU_ARCH` was verified unset at runtime and absent from shell rc files on the
accurate machines, `mx.metal.is_available()` is true, and the device is `Device(gpu, 0)`.

## Additional checks

- **Not a CPU fallback.** On the affected machine the GPU stream differs measurably from the
  CPU stream at M=1, so they are distinct paths.
- **Deterministic.** Repeated GPU runs are bit-identical (`np.array_equal` true), so this is a
  kernel property rather than a race.
- **Confined to matmul.** GPU-vs-CPU on identical fp32 data: matmul 8.105e-04, while `sum`
  1.840e-07, `softmax` 1.143e-07, `rms_norm` 1.123e-07, `sigmoid` 1.213e-07, `exp` 5.961e-08
  and `conv1d` 6.367e-08.
- **Magnitude matches ~11-bit truncation.** A positive control that explicitly truncates operand
  mantissas reproduces the scale: 11 bits gives 1.423e-04 and 10 bits 2.824e-04, bracketing the
  observed 8.302e-04.
- **Shape-gated, not size-gated.** With N = 1 the GPU stays accurate at M = 8 (7.323e-08) and
  M = 256 (9.573e-08). Both dimensions must be >= 2.
- **float32 only.** Relative error against a float64 arbiter, with and without the workaround
  below: fp32 7.608e-04 -> 4.544e-07, but bf16 2.696e-03 both ways and fp16 4.614e-04 both
  ways, i.e. unchanged.

## Workaround, and its cost

`MLX_METAL_GPU_ARCH=applegpu_g14p` restores accuracy (4.544e-07), but it selects an older
architecture for every kernel, not just this one. Measured on the M5 Max at 1024x4096x4096
(TFLOP/s, best of 10 after warmup):

| precision | default `g17s` | `applegpu_g14p` |
|---|---|---|
| fp32 | 39.6 | 13.6 |
| bf16 | 36.7 | 13.9 |
| fp16 | 46.7 | 14.0 |
| q4 | 35.0 | 12.3 |

So it is roughly a 3x throughput cost across the board — usable for verification, not as a
general setting. Running the reference on `mx.stream(mx.cpu)` is the cheaper remedy for
float32 numerical work.

## Why this is easy to miss

M = 1 is accurate, and bf16/fp16/quantized paths are unaffected, so ordinary inference and
serving smoke tests never surface it. It shows up in float32 numerical work — parity harnesses,
float64-arbiter oracles, conversion checks — where it presented to us as a defect in our own
code and cost several rounds of investigation before a float64 arbiter identified which side
was wrong.

## Environment

- Apple M5 Max, macOS 27.0, `applegpu_g17s`
- mlx 0.32.2 (bracket measured across 0.29.3 - 0.32.2), mlx-metal matched
- Cross-checked on Apple M3 Ultra (`applegpu_g15d`, macOS 27.0, mlx 0.32.1) and an M4

items.title: Add multi-point closed-form gradient reference tests
items.body:
### What this adds

A new test file, `python/tests/test_grad_reference.py`, comparing gradients against closed-form derivatives evaluated in float64:

- **15 elementwise ops** (`sin`, `sinh`, `cosh`, `tan`, `arcsin`, `arccos`, `arctan`, `arcsinh`, `arctanh`, `expm1`, `log1p`, `reciprocal`, `rsqrt`, `erf`, `sigmoid`) and **2 binary ops** (`logaddexp`, `arctan2`, both arguments).
- **33 points per op** instead of one or two, over ranges chosen to stay well inside each op's domain and away from poles.
- **Per-dtype tolerances** (`float32` rtol 1e-5, `float16` rtol 5e-3) rather than one generic value. These come from the measured agreement between MLX's float32 gradients and these closed forms on well-conditioned inputs, which sits at about one float32 epsilon (~1.2e-7); the tolerances leave roughly two orders of headroom so ordinary cross-machine rounding never trips them.
- A second-order check on three ops, and a dedicated multi-point `erf` check.

One new file, no changes to existing tests. Runs in ~0.05s, passes on `DEVICE=cpu` and `DEVICE=gpu`.

### Why

The existing autograd tests check a gradient against a hand-written expected value at one or two points. That is a real check, but a defect whose effect depends on the input can sit inside the gap.

`erf` is the clean example. Its derivative is `2/sqrt(pi) * exp(-x^2)`, and the current exact assertion evaluates it at **x = 0**:

```cpp
CHECK_EQ(out.second.item<float>(),
         static_cast<float>(1.12837916709551257389615890312154517));
```

That assertion is tight — it catches an error in the `2/sqrt(pi)` coefficient down to ~1e-6 relative. But at `x = 0` the exponential factor is exactly `1.0`, which is exactly representable in every float format. So anything that goes wrong in *how that factor is computed or stored* — a lower-precision intermediate, a rounded temporary — changes nothing at that point and passes.

Evaluating the same closed form on a grid closes that gap without touching any existing test.

### Evidence it works

I checked the current gradients first: across a sweep of these ops over several input classes, dtypes and both streams, I found **no gradient defects in v0.32.0**. This isn't a bug report — the gradients look healthy, and these tests guard the surface rather than fix anything.

To confirm the tests can detect something, I temporarily introduced two defects locally, one at a time, and reran both suites:

| local defect (temporary, not in this PR) | existing python suite | these tests |
|---|---|---|
| `erf` backward rounds `exp(-x^2)` through float16 (~2.4e-4 relative) | passes | **fails** — `op='erf', dtype=float32`, 30/32 points mismatched, e.g. `0.020661240` vs expected `0.020666985` |
| `arctan` backward rounds `(1+x^2)` through bfloat16 (~2.9e-3 relative) | fails (`test_trig_ops`) | **fails** — `op='arctan', dtype=float32` |

The first is the case that motivated this: a 2.4e-4 relative error in `erf`'s backward pass — four orders of magnitude larger than the coefficient error the x = 0 assertion catches — passes the existing suite because of where it's evaluated. The second is caught by both, which is what you'd expect when a defect is large enough to disturb an existing test.

Both defects were reverted and the tree rebuilt; the tests pass again on clean `v0.32.0`.

### Scope — what these tests do not cover

- **Small defects in float16 / bfloat16.** The legitimate spread between an fp16 gradient and a float64 reference is already ~6e-4 relative (~1e-3 for longer reductions), so a defect below that isn't distinguishable from rounding at that precision. The float16 tolerances here sit above that spread and will only catch coarse errors; bfloat16 isn't covered.
- **Long reductions.** Only elementwise and simple binary ops. Reassociation in a long reduction widens the legitimate spread and would need its own tolerances.
- **Selection ops** (`max`, `abs`, `sort`, `where`, `floor`, …) are deliberately excluded: their derivative isn't unique at ties and kinks, so a reference comparison there tests the tie-breaking convention rather than the gradient.
- **GPU-kernel-specific paths.** The tests run on whichever device is selected, so they exercise Metal under `DEVICE=gpu`, but they compare against a mathematical reference rather than against the CPU result — this isn't a CPU-vs-Metal parity check.
- Ops are covered via their closed form, so anything without a simple analytic derivative is out of scope.
- **The tolerances are deliberately conservative** and can be tightened per-op once there's CI history showing the real cross-machine spread. They're set for margin on hardware I can't test rather than for maximum sensitivity.

Happy to trim the op list, adjust tolerances, or split the file differently if you'd prefer a smaller footprint.

items.title: Add determinant and sign-log-determinant functions to mlx.core.linalg
items.body:
## Proposed changes: Add `linalg.det` and `linalg.slogdet`

Related: https://github.com/ml-explore/mlx/issues/3335

Add determinant (`det`) and sign-log-determinant (`slogdet`) functions to `mlx.core.linalg`.

- `mx.linalg.det(a)` - returns the determinant of a square matrix
- `mx.linalg.slogdet(a)` - returns `(sign, logabsdet)` for numerical stability

## Design Choices

### Composite on `lu_factor()`, no new primitive

Both functions compose on the existing `lu_factor()` primitive rather than introducing a new one. This mirrors how JAX implements `slogdet` and is consistent with how `solve()` already builds on `lu()` in this codebase. 

### `slogdet` as the core, `det` derived from it

`slogdet` is the numerically stable. For the general case (N > 3), `det` simply calls `slogdet` and reconstructs via `sign * exp(logabsdet)`. This avoids duplicating the LU-based logic. An internal `slogdet_impl` function handles the shared logic so the public `det` and `slogdet` entry points each validate and promote types exactly once.

### Small-matrix fast paths (1x1, 2x2, 3x3)

A shared `det_raw_small()` helper computes determinants directly using closed-form formulas (element extraction via slice/squeeze, then the standard cofactor expansion for 3x3). This avoids LU overhead for the small matrices common in batched ML workloads (e.g., 3x3 covariance matrices in normalizing flows).

`det` calls `det_raw_small` directly for N <= 3, skipping the log/exp round-trip entirely. `slogdet` calls it too, then splits the raw result into `sign(raw)` and `log(abs(raw))`.

### Integer auto-promotion

`det`/`slogdet` promote integer inputs to float32 via `at_least_float()`. This matches NumPy's behavior (`np.linalg.det` accepts integer arrays).

### Singular matrix handling

For the LU path, singularity is detected by checking for exact zeros on the U diagonal (same approach as NumPy). Singular matrices return `(sign=0, logabsdet=-inf)` from `slogdet`, and `0.0` from `det`.

Thanks @Lucas-Fernandes-Martins for pointing out the singular matrix [issue](https://github.com/ml-explore/mlx/issues/3335#issuecomment-4255476950) in LU factorization. 

## Testing

- **Correctness**: Compared against `np.linalg.det` / `np.linalg.slogdet` for 1x1 through 5x5, random matrices, identity
- **Batched**: Shapes `(3, 4, 4)` and `(2, 3, 3, 3)` match NumPy
- **Numerical stability**: `0.1 * I_100` (det underflows in float32, slogdet stays finite)
- **Singular matrices**: `sign=0`, `logabsdet=-inf`
- **Consistency**: `sign * exp(logabsdet)` matches `det` for non-singular inputs
- **Dtypes**: float32, float64, integer auto-promotion
- **Error handling**: non-square and 1D inputs raise `ValueError`
- **Full suite**: All 18 existing linalg tests continue to pass (186 subtests)

items.body:
**Describe the bug**

I have observed some subtle differences in the results of MLX's `exp` function compared to other libraries, and even between its CPU and GPU computations.

**To Reproduce**

Include code snippet

```python
import numpy as np
import torch as tf
import mlx.core as mx
import math

print(np.__version__)  # 2.0.0
print(tf.__version__)  # 2.3.1
print(mx.__version__)  # 0.16.1

v = float(-7.773141)
arr = np.array([v])

print(v)                         # -7.773141
print(arr.item())                # -7.773141
print(tf.from_numpy(arr).item()) # -7.773141
print(mx.array(arr).item())      # -7.773140907287598

print(math.exp(v))                                 # 0.0004208891755120154
print(np.exp(arr).item())                          # 0.0004208891755120154
print(tf.exp(tf.from_numpy(arr)).item())           # 0.0004208891755120154
print(mx.exp(mx.array(arr), stream=mx.cpu).item()) # 0.00042088920599780977
print(mx.exp(mx.array(arr), stream=mx.gpu).item()) # 0.0004208892351016402
```

**Expected behavior**

1. The `exp` function in MLX should produce results consistent with other widely-used libraries such as NumPy and PyTorch, at least to a high degree of precision (e.g., matching to 10-12 decimal places).
2. The results of MLX's `exp` function should be consistent across different compute devices (CPU and GPU) for the same input.
3. The conversion of floating-point numbers to MLX arrays should preserve the exact value without any loss of precision.

In general, we expect numerical operations in MLX to produce results that are either identical to or extremely close to those of other established scientific computing libraries, ensuring reproducibility and consistency across different platforms and libraries.

**Desktop (please complete the following information):**

 - OS Version: macOS 15.1 Beta (24B5024e)
 - Version: MLX 0.16.1

**Additional context**

While these differences are small, they could potentially lead to inconsistencies in certain applications, especially those requiring high precision or when accumulating errors over many operations.

items.body: Some ops (exp, sin, cos, erf, erfinv) use the fp32 approximation for double and are hence not so accurate for double precision. Would be good to have specializations of these for double as well.

items.title: Compute float64 exp, sin, cos and erf in double
items.body:
## Proposed changes

Fixes #4158.

`exp`, `sin`, `cos` and `erf` in `mlx/backend/cpu/simd/math.h` are hand-rolled
float32 approximations, and they convert their input to `Simd<float, N>`
unconditionally. float64 therefore gets float32 accuracy:

| max rel. error, float64 | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `exp` | 3.00e-07 | 0.00e+00 |
| `sin` | 7.75e-07 | 0.00e+00 |
| `cos` | 3.42e-04 | 0.00e+00 |
| `erf` | 9.44e-04 | 0.00e+00 |

`exp` is worse than imprecise, because it also inherited float's saturation
points, so a float64 array returns the wrong value outright:

```
exp(100.0)  -> inf   (should be 2.688e+43)
exp(709.0)  -> inf   (should be 8.218e+307)
exp(-200.0) -> 0     (should be 1.384e-87)
```

This routes double through libm and leaves float32 untouched.

Worth flagging: the existing `test_unary_ops` in `python/tests/test_double.py`
asserts `allclose(y, y_double.astype(mx.float32, mx.cpu))` — it compares the
float64 result against the float32 one, so it could not catch any of this.

### Performance

This is a real cost. 2^20 elements, M2 Pro, best of 7 runs:

| | float32 (unchanged) | float64 before | float64 after |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `exp` | 0.437 -> 0.438 ms | 0.573 ms | 5.908 ms |
| `sin` | 0.804 -> 0.807 ms | 1.067 ms | 6.659 ms |
| `cos` | 0.786 -> 0.791 ms | 1.032 ms | 6.743 ms |
| `erf` | 0.877 -> 0.878 ms | 1.160 ms | 11.641 ms |

float32 is unchanged, as expected from a compile-time branch. The old float64
speed was the speed of computing the wrong answer.

I checked whether that speed can be recovered. Accelerate's vectorized double
math (`simd::exp` / `simd::erf` on `double4`) measured no faster than scalar
libm on this machine — 2.456 vs 2.558 ms for `exp`, 9.653 vs 9.951 ms for `erf`,
with bit-identical results — so the cost looks intrinsic to evaluating these at
double precision rather than a poor choice of implementation. Happy to take
direction if you would prefer a different trade-off here.

`erfinv` still narrows to float. It has no libm equivalent and would need a
double precision polynomial, so I left it for a separate change rather than
half-do it.

### Testing

Two new tests in `python/tests/test_double.py`: one pins the four ops to double
accuracy against numpy, one pins the range of `exp`. Both fail before this
change and pass after.

- Full Python suite: 821 tests, no new failures.
- Full C++ suite: 247 cases, 3326 assertions, all pass.

Built CPU-only (`MLX_BUILD_METAL=OFF`). float64 is CPU-only in MLX, so that is
where this behaviour lives, but note the GPU suite was not run on my machine.

## Checklist

- [x] I have read the [CONTRIBUTING](https://github.com/ml-explore/mlx/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md) document
- [x] I have run `pre-commit run --all-files` to format my code / installed pre-commit prior to committing changes
- [x] I have added tests that prove my fix is effective or that my feature works
- [ ] I have updated the necessary documentation (if needed) — no documentation change needed, there is no API change

items.title: [BUG] `x ** 2` is less accurate than `x * x` (0.938 vs 0.500 ULP) and is lane-dependent
items.body:
**Describe the bug**
`x ** 2` (and `mx.power(x, 2)`) route through a general power kernel instead of a multiply. In float32 it is worse than `x * x` on 9742/20000 random draws and better on zero. On float64 it is lane-dependent. `mx.square(x)` is already bit-identical to `x * x` in both precisions, and behaves correctly. `**` just is not reaching it.

**To Reproduce**

```python
import mlx.core as mx, numpy as np, mpmath as mp
mp.mp.dps = 60
rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
xs = rng.uniform(-3, 3, 20000)

with mx.stream(mx.cpu):
    A = mx.array(xs, dtype=mx.float64)
    sq, mul, pw = mx.square(A), A * A, A ** 2
    mx.eval(sq, mul, pw)
print("float64: mx.square == x*x :", np.array_equal(np.asarray(sq), np.asarray(mul)))
print("float64: x**2      == x*x :", np.array_equal(np.asarray(pw), np.asarray(mul)),
      f"({int((np.asarray(pw) != np.asarray(mul)).sum())}/20000 differ)")

x32 = mx.array(xs.astype(np.float32))
print("float32: x**2 == x*x :", np.array_equal(np.asarray(x32 ** 2), np.asarray(x32 * x32)),
      f"({int((np.asarray(x32**2) != np.asarray(x32*x32)).sum())}/20000 differ)")

def ulps(g):
    return max(abs(float((mp.mpf(float(g[i])) - mp.mpf(float(xs[i]))**2)
                         / mp.mpf(np.spacing(abs(np.float64(g[i])))))) for i in range(2000))
print(f"float64 max |ULP| : x*x {ulps(np.asarray(mul)):.3f}   mx.square {ulps(np.asarray(sq)):.3f}   "
      f"x**2 {ulps(np.asarray(pw)):.3f}")
```


```
float64: mx.square == x*x : True
float64: x**2      == x*x : False   (2620/20000 differ)
float32: x**2      == x*x : False   (9742/20000 differ)
float64 max |ULP| : x*x 0.500   mx.square 0.500   x**2 0.938
```

**Expected behavior**
`x ** 2` should be as accurate as `x * x`, i.e. lowered to a multiply. Likewise `x ** 3` → `x*x*x`,
`x ** 0.5` → `sqrt`, `x ** -1` → reciprocal (lane-dependent submitted as a separate issue).
(`x**0.5` on 110/400, `x**-1` on 51/400).


For **exponent 3 and 1.5** the naive algebraic expansion is slightly *worse* than the current power kernel
at the extremes, over 2000 draws vs mpmath:

| exponent | `mx.power` mean/max ULP | algebraic mean/max ULP |
|---|---|---|
| 1.5 | 0.334 / 0.979 | `x*mx.sqrt(x)` 0.347 / **1.165** |
| 3   | 0.344 / 0.979 | `x*x*x` 0.343 / **1.229** |

items.title: The compiler cache and tracing state are process-global and unsynchronized in 0.31.x — is the 0.32 thread-local redesign the intended thread-safety contract?
items.body:
## Summary

In 0.31.x, three pieces of state that every `compile()` call touches are process-global
with no synchronization: the compiler cache, the tracing stack, and the counters behind
`in_tracing()` / `retain_graph()`. Any binding that lets two threads call a compiled
function has to serialize *all* of it itself, and the serialization has to span the whole
trace rather than just the cache lookup, because tracing state is global too.

Reading the 0.32.0 and 0.32.1 headers and shipped binaries, it looks like this was
addressed — by making the cache and the tracing state `thread_local`, and (in 0.32.1) by
putting the per-thread cache behind a `shared_ptr` so the erase path can hold a `weak_ptr`
to it. I could not find that written down anywhere, so this issue is mostly asking whether
that is a deliberate, supported thread-safety contract that bindings can rely on, or an
incidental consequence of another change. The rest is the detail I gathered, in case it is
useful.

Versions I read:

* **0.31.1** — full C++ sources, as vendored into `mlx-swift` (`Source/Cmlx/mlx`).
  All `file:line` references below are to this tree unless stated otherwise.
* **0.32.0** and **0.32.1** — headers and `libmlx.dylib` from the published wheels. I do
  not have the `.cpp` files for these, so the 0.32 claims come from headers plus the
  symbol table (specifically, which symbols land in `__DATA,__thread_vars` /
  `__DATA,__thread_bss`). I have flagged each one with how it was established.

---

## 1. What the 0.31.x code does

### 1.1 `CompilerCache` has no mutex, and `find()` hands out a reference held across the whole trace

`compile.cpp:298-384`. The cache is `std::unordered_map<std::uintptr_t,
std::vector<CacheEntry>> cache_` (`:383`), reached through a function-local singleton:

```cpp
// compile.cpp:386-389
CompilerCache& compiler_cache() {
  static CompilerCache compiler_cache_;
  return compiler_cache_;
}
```

There is no mutex in the class, and `grep -n 'mutex\|lock_guard\|atomic\|thread_local'
mlx/compile.cpp mlx/transforms.cpp mlx/transforms_impl.h` returns nothing.

`find()` is a mutating lookup on both levels:

```cpp
// compile.cpp:313-321
// Returns a reference to a CacheEntry which can be updated
// by the caller to avoid copying large tapes / inputs / outputs
CacheEntry& find(std::uintptr_t fun_id, ...) {
  std::vector<CacheEntry>& entries = cache_[fun_id];   // insert; may rehash
  ...
  entries.push_back(CacheEntry{stream, shapeless});    // :363 — may reallocate
  return entries.back();                               // :364
}
```

The comment at `:313-314` is the important part: the returned reference is deliberately
long-lived. The single caller holds it across the entire compile:

```cpp
// compile.cpp:1116
auto& entry = compiler_cache().find(fun_id, inputs, shapeless, constants);
```

and then writes and reads through it at `:1119` (`entry.empty`), `:1121-1127`
(`entry.constants`, `entry.inputs`, `entry.outputs`, `entry.extra` — filled by
`compile_trace`, which calls back into user code), `:1132` (`entry.tape`), `:1137`
(`compile_simplify`), `:1144` (`compile_fuse`), and finally `:1150-1153`
(`compile_replace(entry.tape, entry.inputs, entry.outputs, ...)` and `entry.extra`).

Erase and clear are bare:

```cpp
// compile.cpp:367-373
void erase(std::uintptr_t fun_id) { cache_.erase(fun_id); }
void clear() { cache_.clear(); }
```

Two things follow that are worth separating, because one of them is often assumed away.
A rehash of `cache_` caused by another key's insertion does **not** invalidate the
`std::vector<CacheEntry>&` — `unordered_map` rehashing invalidates iterators but not
references to elements. The real hazards are: (i) concurrent unsynchronized modification
of the map is a data race in its own right regardless of reference stability; (ii)
`entries.push_back` at `:363` reallocating the vector invalidates a `CacheEntry&` another
thread is compiling into; (iii) `erase(fun_id)` destroys that vector outright, so an
in-flight `CacheEntry&` becomes a reference to a destroyed object.

One more detail: the cache key includes `default_stream(default_device())` (`:346`), and
at 0.31.x the default stream lives in the process-global `Scheduler` singleton
(`scheduler.h:159`, reached via `scheduler.cpp:9-15`), so it is shared too.

### 1.2 Tracing state is process-global, not per-thread

```cpp
// transforms.cpp:45-50
std::vector<std::pair<char, char>>& detail::InTracing::trace_stack() {
  static std::vector<std::pair<char, char>> trace_stack_;   // not thread_local
  return trace_stack_;
}
int detail::InTracing::grad_counter{0};                      // not thread_local
int detail::RetainGraph::tracing_counter{0};                 // not thread_local
```

`InTracing`'s constructor and destructor `push_back`/`pop_back` that vector and adjust
`grad_counter` (`transforms_impl.h:24-32`), so two threads entering any transform at the
same time race on a `std::vector` and on a plain `int`. The destructor also reads
`trace_stack().back().second` (`transforms_impl.h:30`) *before* popping, which is only
correct if the stack is that thread's own.

`in_dynamic_tracing()` makes the assumption explicit — `transforms_impl.h:37-40` reads
`trace_stack().front().first` under the comment "compile is always and only the outer-most
transform". With a shared stack, `front()` may be a different thread's entry.

Everything that reads this state is therefore affected by what other threads are doing.
The complete set in 0.31.1:

| Site | Reads | Effect when another thread is tracing |
|---|---|---|
| `array.cpp:163-166` `array::is_tracer()` | `in_tracing()`, `retain_graph()` | feeds all four rows below |
| `transforms.cpp:97-99` | `is_tracer()` | `async_eval` throws "[async_eval] Not allowed inside a graph transformation." |
| `transforms.cpp:102-106` | `is_tracer()` | `eval` throws "Attempting to eval an array during function transformations…" |
| `transforms.cpp:144-147`, `:277-279` | `is_tracer()` | `eval` skips `detach()` — the graph is retained instead of freed |
| `backend/{cpu,cuda,metal}/eval.cpp:18/33/38` | `is_tracer()` | inputs are pinned against donation |
| `fast.cpp:825` | `in_grad_tracing()` | `scaled_dot_product_attention` sets `is_training`, changing which kernel runs and whether `logsumexp` is produced |
| `ops.cpp:1495`, `:1549`, `:6021` | `in_dynamic_tracing()` | `broadcast_arrays`, `broadcast_to`, `number_of_elements` build dynamic-shape graph nodes instead of folding shapes |

And the writers: `compile_trace` (`compile.cpp:397`), `vjp` (`transforms.cpp:333`), `jvp`
(`:531`), `vmap_trace` (`:699`), and `RetainGraph` around each `primitive().vjp(...)`
(`:478`).

The `fast.cpp:825` row is the one I would point at first, because it needs no data race at
all to misbehave: one thread computing gradients flips `is_training` for every other
thread's attention call, deterministically, for as long as the gradient trace is alive.

### 1.3 The `compile()` deleter erases the cache unlocked, from an arbitrary thread

```cpp
// compile.cpp:1206-1212
auto pfun = std::shared_ptr<std::function<...>>(
    new std::function<...>{fun},
    [](auto* p) {
      detail::compile_erase(reinterpret_cast<std::uintptr_t>(p));
      delete p;
    });
```

`compile_erase` is `compiler_cache().erase(fun_id)` (`:1184-1186`). The deleter runs
wherever the last `shared_ptr` reference happens to drop, which is not necessarily the
thread that compiled, and takes no lock — so it is an unsynchronized `unordered_map::erase`
against concurrent `find()`. It is also the one erase site a binding cannot wrap, since it
is internal to `mlx::core::compile()`.

---

## 2. What this means for an embedder

**The race.** Two threads calling different compiled functions for the first time both
enter `CompilerCache::find`, both execute `cache_[fun_id]` at `:321`, and modify the same
`unordered_map` concurrently — bucket array, size, and node links, with no happens-before
between them. That alone is undefined behavior; in practice it shows up as a lost entry,
a corrupted bucket chain, or a crash inside `__hash_table::__do_rehash`. Two threads
calling the *same* compiled function for the first time are worse: both can observe
`entry.empty == true` at `:1119`, both set it false, and both then write `entry.inputs`,
`entry.outputs`, `entry.tape` and `entry.extra` through the same reference while
`compile_trace` interleaves their graph construction. And because `find()` returns a
reference the caller keeps for the whole of `compile_trace` → `compile_dfs` →
`compile_simplify` → `compile_fuse` → `compile_replace`, a concurrent `push_back` at `:363`
or an `erase` from §1.3 can move or destroy the entry out from under a compile that is
still filling it. The tracing stack races independently and for the same reason. None of
this is a narrow interleaving — the compile path is long, and the window is the whole of
it.

**The serialization it forces.** Because the tracing flag is global rather than per-thread,
a binding cannot fix this by locking only the cache lookup: while any thread is inside
`compile_trace`, `in_tracing()` is true for every thread, so every other thread's `eval`
must also be excluded or it will retain graphs it should detach (`transforms.cpp:144-147`)
and may throw (`:97-106`). The only sound discipline available to a binding is a single
process-wide lock held across the entire compiled call *and* every `eval`/`async_eval`.
That is what mlx-swift does — its `evalLock` is exactly this — and the cost is that no two
compiled calls, and no compiled call and any eval, can ever overlap, on any stream or
device. That ceiling is the real consequence: not a rare crash, but a structural cap on
concurrent multi-stream use that the binding has no way to lift on its own. It also has a
sharp edge. A companion pull request against `ml-explore/mlx-swift` describes a permanent
deadlock in that package: the per-`CompiledFunction` `NSLock` and the global `evalLock`
end up acquired in opposite orders on different threads, because `compile_trace` calls back
into Swift while `evalLock` is held and the callee is another compiled function that takes
its own instance lock first. Every `MLXNN` activation is a file-scope compiled function, so
any traced body that calls `silu(x)` is a nesting site; two threads, one nested and one
plain, wedge on first use. That PR's fix — one global lock order, `evalLock` outermost —
resolves the deadlock but deliberately keeps the full serialization, precisely because
§1.2 means it cannot be narrowed from the Swift side.

---

## 3. What 0.32.0 and 0.32.1 appear to have changed

This is the part I would most like confirmed, since I am reading headers and symbol tables
rather than sources.

### 0.32.0

`transforms_impl.h`, diffed against 0.31.1 — two one-word changes and one addition:

```
-  static int grad_counter;                 (InTracing)
+  static thread_local int grad_counter;
-  static int tracing_counter;              (RetainGraph)
+  static thread_local int tracing_counter;
+  struct InExportTracing { ... static int& counter(); };
```

`trace_stack()`'s declaration is unchanged, so the header cannot say whether its local
static became thread-local — but the binary can. In 0.32.0's `libmlx.dylib`, all of these
are in `__DATA,__thread_vars` / `__DATA,__thread_bss`:

```
__ZZN3mlx4core6detail9InTracing11trace_stackEvE12trace_stack_
__ZN3mlx4core6detail9InTracing12grad_counterE
__ZN3mlx4core6detail11RetainGraph15tracing_counterE
__ZZN3mlx4core6detail15InExportTracing7counterEvE8counter_
__ZZN3mlx4core6detail14compiler_cacheEvE15compiler_cache_
```

So in 0.32.0 the tracing stack, both counters, **and the compiler cache singleton itself**
are thread-local. For comparison, the only `thread_local` anywhere in 0.31.1's core outside
the backends is in the bundled pocketfft.

The same symbol dump shows `default_stream_storage` and `stream_from_thread_local_stream`
in `__thread_vars` as well, i.e. default streams became per-thread too — which matters here
because the cache key includes the default stream (`compile.cpp:346`).

### 0.32.1

`compile_impl.h` changes shape:

```
-MLX_API void compile_erase(std::uintptr_t fun_id);
-MLX_API bool compile_cache_empty();
-MLX_API void compile_clear_cache();
+// Get the compiler cache of current thread.
+class CompileCache;
+using CompileCacheWeakPtr = std::weak_ptr<CompileCache>;
+MLX_API CompileCacheWeakPtr compile_cache();
+MLX_API void compile_erase(const CompileCacheWeakPtr& cache, std::uintptr_t fun_id);
+MLX_API void compile_clear_cache(const CompileCacheWeakPtr& cache);
```

and the 0.32.1 symbol table fills in the rest: `CompilerCache` is renamed
`detail::CompileCache`; the raw per-thread accessor is `detail::compile_cache_unsafe()`
whose local static `cache` is thread-local; the map is now
`unordered_map<uintptr_t, shared_ptr<vector<CacheEntry>>>`; the cache object is
`make_shared<CompileCache>()`; and `find` returns a
`tuple<CacheEntry&, shared_ptr<vector<CacheEntry>>>` — a reference plus an owning handle
that keeps the entry vector alive for as long as the caller holds it.

Between them those two releases look like they close all three items in §1: the race is
gone because nothing is shared; the reference-across-the-trace problem is handled by
returning the owning `shared_ptr` alongside the reference; and the deleter problem is
handled by having it capture a `weak_ptr` to the cache of the thread that compiled, so it
erases from the right cache or from none at all if that thread is gone.

### What I would like to know

1. **Is this intended and supported?** Concretely: may a binding now assume that
   `compile()` and the transforms are safe to call from multiple threads concurrently, or
   is thread-locality here an implementation detail that could be reverted? Bindings are
   holding process-wide locks on the strength of the old behavior, and will not drop them
   without something to point at.
2. **Documentation.** There is nothing in the docs stating which entry points are
   thread-safe. Even one paragraph — "the compiler cache and tracing state are per-thread;
   `array` and the scheduler are not / are" — would let embedders size their locks
   correctly. `compile_cache_unsafe()` suggests the distinction is already understood
   internally.
3. **Cost of per-thread caches.** Thread-local means no reuse across threads: N worker
   threads pay N full traces (`compile_trace` + `compile_dfs` + `compile_simplify` +
   `compile_fuse`) and hold N tapes. For an embedder whose compiled functions are
   process-wide singletons — mlx-swift's `MLXNN` activations are file-scope globals — that
   is N× first-call latency and N× tape residency. Was a shared cache under a mutex
   considered and rejected on complexity grounds, or is a shared cache still open?
4. **Per-thread default streams.** Since 0.32 the default stream is thread-local and is
   part of the cache key, so two threads calling the same compiled function land on
   different streams by default. That seems right, but it is a behavior change worth a
   release note.
5. **Backport.** 0.31.x is what a number of downstreams are pinned to, including
   `mlx-swift`, which vendors 0.31.1. Is a note on the 0.31 line worth it, or is "upgrade
   to 0.32.1" the answer?

---

## 4. Fix options, if any of the above is still open

Recorded mainly for the shared-cache question in (3).

**A. A mutex on `CompilerCache`.** The obvious shape, and the one that preserves
cross-thread reuse. The complication is `find()`'s contract: it returns a `CacheEntry&`
that the caller holds through the entire compile, so a `std::lock_guard` inside `find()`
protects nothing that matters. Three ways out, in increasing order of appeal:

* *Return a copy.* Defeats the stated purpose of the reference (`compile.cpp:313-314`) —
  copying tapes, inputs and outputs is exactly what it exists to avoid.
* *Return a locked handle.* `find()` returns an RAII object owning the lock; the caller
  holds it to `:1153`. Correct and small, but it makes the whole compile a critical
  section, so concurrent first-use compiles of *different* functions serialize — better
  than today, still a bottleneck, and it needs care against re-entrancy (a traced body
  that calls another compiled function; note `:1108-1113` already short-circuits that case
  before touching the cache, so a recursive mutex may not even be needed, but the
  interaction should be deliberate rather than incidental).
* *Lock only the lookup, make entries independently owned.* Guard `cache_` with a mutex
  and store `shared_ptr<vector<CacheEntry>>` as the mapped type, so the map can rehash and
  `erase` can run while an outstanding entry stays alive. This is, as far as I can tell,
  exactly the ownership model 0.32.1 adopted — just with a mutex over one shared map
  instead of a thread-local map per thread. A per-entry `once_flag` or state enum would
  then be needed so that two threads racing on the same cold entry produce one trace rather
  than two.

**B. `thread_local` tracing stack.** Independent of A and, I would argue, necessary
regardless: without it the serialization in §2 cannot be narrowed even if the cache itself
is made safe, because `in_tracing()` leaks across threads. The things that assume
process-global tracing are enumerated in the table in §1.2; reading them again with
`thread_local` in mind, none of them wants the global reading — `is_tracer()`,
`in_grad_tracing()` and `in_dynamic_tracing()` are all asking "am *I* under a transform?",
and every one of them gets a wrong answer when the answer comes from another thread. The
only care needed is that a transform's trace and the evals it triggers stay on one thread,
which they do: `compile_trace` (`compile.cpp:397`), `vjp` (`transforms.cpp:333`), `jvp`
(`:531`) and `vmap_trace` (`:699`) all scope `InTracing` to a single synchronous call
frame. This is what 0.32.0 did.

**C. Lifetime-safe erase.** Whatever A resolves to, the deleter at `compile.cpp:1209-1212`
must take the same lock, or hold a weak handle to the cache it is erasing from. It is the
one path a binding cannot wrap. 0.32.1's `weak_ptr<CompileCache>` handles it.

**D. Can Python users hit any of this?** Honestly: mostly no on a GIL build, and the
reason is worth stating because it explains why this surfaced in a Swift binding rather
than in Python. In 0.31.1's bindings, the compile path never releases the GIL —
`PyCompiledFun::call_impl` calls `mx::detail::compile(...)(inputs)` directly
(`python/src/transforms.cpp:558`), and `~PyCompiledFun` calls `compile_erase`
(`:580-583`) with the GIL held as usual for a destructor. So §1.1 and §1.3 are effectively
serialized by the interpreter. `mx.eval` and `mx.async_eval` *do* release it
(`python/src/transforms.cpp:1171`, `:1191`), so §1.2 is reachable: a thread computing
gradients holds `grad_counter > 0` across its Python callback, and any other thread that
calls `mx.fast.scaled_dot_product_attention` in that window gets `is_training == true`
(`fast.cpp:825`) and a different kernel. That one needs no data race and no free-threading.
On a free-threaded build (3.13t / 3.14t) the GIL argument disappears entirely and the
compile-path races become reachable directly — so if free-threaded wheels are planned, the
0.32 work is load-bearing for them. I could not check whether such wheels are published;
the wheel I have is `cp312-cp312-macosx_26_0_arm64`.

---

## 5. Reproduction

None of the below has been run — they are sketches for someone with a build. All are
written to fail on 0.31.x and pass on 0.32.x, so they double as a check on §3.

**R1 — the cache race (TSan).** Two threads, two distinct `fun_id`s, so both take the
`cache_[fun_id]` insert path at `compile.cpp:321`; a fresh input shape each iteration
forces the cold path at `:1119` every time.

```cpp
// build against mlx with -fsanitize=thread
#include <thread>
#include <vector>
#include "mlx/mlx.h"
namespace mx = mlx::core;

std::vector<mx::array> f(const std::vector<mx::array>& x) {
  return {mx::exp(mx::negative(mx::sum(x[0])))};
}
std::vector<mx::array> g(const std::vector<mx::array>& x) {
  return {mx::square(mx::add(x[0], x[0]))};
}

int main() {
  auto cf = mx::compile(f);
  auto cg = mx::compile(g);
  auto run = [](auto fn, float v) {
    for (int i = 1; i <= 128; ++i) {
      auto x = mx::full({i}, v, mx::float32);   // new shape => new CacheEntry
      mx::eval(fn({x}));
    }
  };
  std::thread t1(run, cf, 1.0f), t2(run, cg, 2.0f);
  t1.join(); t2.join();
}
```

Expected on 0.31.x: TSan races on `CompilerCache::cache_` and on
`InTracing::trace_stack_`; without TSan, intermittent crashes in the hash table. Expected
on 0.32.x: clean.

**R2 — the erase/find interleaving.** Same shape, but thread B churns compiled-function
lifetimes so `compile_erase` runs concurrently with thread A's `find`:

```cpp
std::thread a([]{ /* R1's `run`, one function, 500 iterations */ });
std::thread b([]{
  for (int i = 0; i < 500; ++i) {
    auto h = mx::compile([](const std::vector<mx::array>& x) {
      return std::vector<mx::array>{mx::abs(x[0])};
    });                                   // lambda => no addressable target
    mx::eval(h({mx::full({4}, 1.0f, mx::float32)}));
  }                                       // dtor => shared_ptr deleter => compile_erase
});
```

The lambda matters: `get_function_address` (`compile.cpp:288-296`) returns 0 for it, which
is what selects the `shared_ptr`-deleter branch at `:1205-1220`.

**R3 — the tracing flag, no sanitizer needed.** This one is a plain wrong answer rather
than UB, and it reproduces from Python on a stock GIL build:

```python
import threading, mlx.core as mx

stop = False

def grads():                       # holds grad_counter > 0 across its Python callback
    f = lambda x: mx.sum(mx.exp(x))
    x = mx.random.normal((256, 256)); mx.eval(x)
    while not stop:
        mx.eval(mx.grad(f)(x))

t = threading.Thread(target=grads); t.start()
# meanwhile, on the main thread, call mx.fast.scaled_dot_product_attention and
# observe `is_training` (fast.cpp:825) flip with the other thread's activity --
# a different kernel is selected and logsumexp is produced, for an inference-only call.
stop = True; t.join()
```

Expected on 0.31.x: the attention call's behavior depends on whether the other thread is
mid-gradient. Expected on 0.32.x: no dependence, since `grad_counter` is thread-local.

---

## Appendix — how the 0.32 claims were established

I did not have 0.32 sources, so for the record:

* `transforms_impl.h` and `compile_impl.h` were diffed directly, 0.31.1 → 0.32.0 → 0.32.1.
* Thread-locality was read off `nm -m libmlx.dylib`: a `thread_local` function-local static
  lands in `__DATA,__thread_vars` with a `$tlv$init` counterpart in `__DATA,__thread_bss`,
  and a non-thread-local one does not. 0.32.0 and 0.32.1 both place `trace_stack_`,
  `grad_counter`, `tracing_counter`, `InExportTracing::counter_`, the compiler-cache
  singleton, and the default-stream storage there; 0.31.1's sources contain no
  `thread_local` in these files at all.
* The 0.32.1 cache redesign was read from demangled symbol names —
  `detail::CompileCache::find(...)`, `detail::compile_erase(std::weak_ptr<CompileCache>
  const&, unsigned long)`, `detail::compile_cache_unsafe()`, and the
  `unordered_map<unsigned long, shared_ptr<vector<CompileCache::CacheEntry>>>`
  instantiations — plus the header declarations quoted above. Anything I could not
  establish this way is phrased as a question, not a claim.

items.title: Fix cpu exclusive scan for complex numbers
items.body:
An exclusive scan writes the identity of its operation into the first position. On the CPU that identity is picked like this:

```cpp
auto init = (issubdtype(in.dtype(), floating))
    ? static_cast<U>(std::numeric_limits<float>::infinity())
    : std::numeric_limits<U>::max();
```

`complex64` is `inexact` but not `floating`, so it takes the second branch. `std::numeric_limits` has no specialization for `complex64_t`, so `max()` returns a value initialized `complex64_t`, which is `0+0j`. Complex comparison is lexicographic on the real part, so that zero beats every negative real part and the scan never recovers:

```python
>>> a = mx.array([-3+1j, -1+2j, -4+0j, -5+5j])
>>> mx.cummax(a, axis=0, inclusive=True)
array([-3+1j, -1+2j, -1+2j, -1+2j], dtype=complex64)
>>> mx.cummax(a, axis=0, inclusive=False)
array([0+0j, 0+0j, 0+0j, 0+0j], dtype=complex64)
```

`cummin` goes the same way whenever the data is non negative, and `logcumsumexp` starts from `0+0j` instead of `-inf`:

```python
>>> b = mx.array([3+1j, 1+2j, 4+0j, 0+5j, 2-1j])
>>> mx.cummin(b, axis=0, inclusive=False)
array([0+0j, 0+0j, 0+0j, 0+0j, 0+0j], dtype=complex64)
```

The inclusive results are correct throughout, so the two disagree: an exclusive scan should equal the inclusive one shifted by a position, and for complex it does not.

Neither GPU backend has this problem: both Metal (`mlx/backend/metal/kernels/utils.h`) and CUDA (`mlx/backend/cuda/device/utils.cuh`) specialize `Limits<complex_t<T>>` to an infinite pair, so `CumMax` there already starts from `{-inf, -inf}` and `CumMin` from `{inf, inf}`. The CPU was the only backend without it. This gives the CPU the same identity. `scan_extreme` replaces the three copies of the ternary, and picks the pair `{inf, inf}` for complex so the identity also wins against an input whose real part is itself infinite, which a bare `inf+0j` would lose to on the imaginary tiebreak.

`logcumsumexp` keeps its own ternary, widened to `inexact` so complex reaches `-inf`. It deliberately does not use `scan_extreme`: its identity has to compare equal to the `minval == -inf` test inside `LogAddExp`, and an infinite imaginary part would fail that and produce NaN.

Verified that exclusive equals inclusive shifted by one across `cumsum`, `cumprod`, `cummax`, `cummin` and `logcumsumexp`, over 8 dtypes, shapes `(7,)`, `(3,5)`, `(2,3,4)`, `(1,)` and `(9,2)`, every axis, and both scan directions. Complex goes from broken to matching; the real dtypes are byte identical to before and still match numpy.

Out of scope and left alone: `logcumsumexp` on an unsigned integer input starts from 0 because there is no representable `-inf`, which is a different problem and predates this.

CPU only. `test_ops.py`, `test_reduce.py`, `test_array.py`, `test_compile.py`, `test_vmap.py`, `test_autograd.py`, `test_nn.py` and the C++ suite (249 cases, 3350 assertions) pass. The added test fails on main with `cummax reverse=False`.

I am a freshman working through this codebase and I used Claude Code alongside it. Every result above came from a run here.
